title: World War II
bigQuestion: What did it take to win the Second World War, and what did the United States become in winning it?

story.title: The Squash Court Under the Stands
story.kicker: On a cold afternoon in December 1942, in a disused squash court beneath the football stands of the University of Chicago, forty-nine people watched the atomic age begin.
paragraphs: Stagg Field on the South Side of Chicago had not hosted a big game in years. Under its west stands, behind a locked door, was an old squash court with a concrete floor. Through the fall of 1942 a team led by the Italian physicist Enrico Fermi had been stacking graphite bricks there, layer on layer, with lumps of uranium set into them. The pile grew to a rough black sphere the size of a two-story house. They called it Chicago Pile-1. No one on the university's board had been told exactly what was being built under the stadium.

The idea was simple to state and terrifying to test. When a uranium atom splits, it throws out neutrons. If those neutrons hit other uranium atoms and split them too, you get a *chain reaction*. Slow it with graphite and control it with rods of cadmium that soak up neutrons, and you have a steady source of energy. Let it run wild and you have a bomb. Fermi's job was to prove that a controlled chain reaction could actually be made to happen. If his calculations were wrong, the pile could run away in a room in the middle of a city of three million people.

On Wednesday, December 2, 1942, the team gathered on a balcony overlooking the pile. Fermi ordered the control rods pulled out a few inches at a time. Counters clicked faster with each step. At each stage he checked his slide rule against the readings and called out what the next step should show. Around 3:25 in the afternoon he ordered the last rod withdrawn, and the clicking rose to a steady roar. The reaction was sustaining itself. After about four and a half minutes, Fermi ordered the rods pushed back in, and the counters slowed. Someone opened a bottle of wine and poured it into paper cups.

One of the leaders telephoned a colleague in Washington with a coded message: the Italian navigator had landed in the new world. The natives, he added, were friendly. Within three years the work begun under those stands had become the Manhattan Project, a secret effort employing well over a hundred thousand people in cities that did not appear on any map. In August 1945 it ended the war with two bombs that killed well over a hundred thousand people in Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

This chapter is about that war: how a country that wanted to stay out of it came to fight on two oceans, what it asked of the people at home, whom it locked up, whom it failed to save, and what it became by winning. The squash court is a good place to start, because everything about the war is in it: brilliance, secrecy, fear, and a decision whose consequences no one at that balcony could see.
story.think: Fermi ran the experiment in a crowded city because the war made waiting impossible. When, if ever, does urgency justify a risk that would be unacceptable in peacetime?

lessons.title: Staying Out
lessons.mainIdea: Most Americans in the 1930s wanted no part of another European war, and Congress wrote that wish into law until Roosevelt found ways around it.
reading: In 1934 a Senate committee spent months investigating why the United States had entered World War I. Its conclusion, that bankers and arms makers had pushed the country toward war for profit, was too simple, but millions believed it. More than a hundred thousand Americans had died in a war that seemed to have settled nothing. Between 1935 and 1937 Congress passed a series of *Neutrality Acts* that banned selling arms or lending money to any country at war. The idea was that if the United States sold nothing and owed nothing, it could not be dragged in again.

Meanwhile the world was coming apart. Japan invaded China in 1937. Adolf Hitler, who had taken power in Germany in 1933, took Austria in 1938 and Czechoslovakia in 1939. On September 1, 1939, Germany invaded Poland, and Britain and France declared war. By June 1940 France had fallen and Britain stood alone, bombed nightly. Roosevelt believed the United States could not stay out, but a large *isolationist* movement, led by figures like the aviator Charles Lindbergh and strong in the Midwest, argued that America should defend its own hemisphere and nothing more. The Chicago Tribune was the movement's loudest newspaper.

Roosevelt moved step by step. In 1940 he traded fifty old destroyers to Britain for naval bases and pushed through the first peacetime draft in American history. In March 1941 Congress passed *Lend-Lease*, which let the president lend weapons and supplies to any country whose defense he judged vital to the United States. Roosevelt compared it to lending a garden hose to a neighbor whose house was on fire. Over the war Lend-Lease sent about fifty billion dollars in aid, mostly to Britain and the Soviet Union. By the fall of 1941 American warships were escorting convoys and being fired on by German submarines.

In a January 1941 speech Roosevelt described a world worth fighting for, one built on four freedoms: of speech, of worship, from want and from fear. He was preparing the country for a war it had not yet entered. Historians debate how far he led public opinion and how far he followed it. What is clear is that in November 1941 most Americans still hoped to stay out, and one Sunday morning ended that hope.

words.d: laws of 1935 to 1937 banning arms sales and loans to countries at war
someone who believes the United States should stay out of other countries' wars
the 1941 law that let the president lend weapons and supplies to countries fighting the Axis
the alliance of Germany, Italy and Japan in World War II

look.title: Four Freedoms
look.text: Roosevelt told Congress he looked forward to a world founded on four essential human freedoms: freedom of speech and expression, freedom of every person to worship in their own way, freedom from want, and freedom from fear, everywhere in the world.
look.cite: Franklin D. Roosevelt, Annual Message to Congress, January 6, 1941 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Two of the freedoms are things government must not do; two are things government must provide. Which is which, and why might the second pair have been controversial at home?

check.q: What did the Neutrality Acts try to prevent?
choices: Immigration from Germany
The United States being pulled into war through arms sales and loans
Japan invading China
Trade with Britain in peacetime
check.why: Many believed profits from arms and loans had dragged the country into World War I.

check.q: How did Roosevelt explain Lend-Lease?
choices: As a way to make money from the war
As a loan that Britain would repay with gold
As lending a hose to a neighbor whose house is on fire
As a treaty with the Soviet Union
check.why: The garden hose image argued that helping Britain was self-defense, not charity or profit.

check.q: Where was the isolationist movement especially strong?
choices: In the Midwest, including Chicago
In New York City
In the Navy
In Hawaii
check.why: Figures like Lindbergh and papers like the Chicago Tribune led the argument to stay out.

lessons.title: Pearl Harbor
lessons.mainIdea: Japan's surprise attack on December 7, 1941, ended the debate over neutrality in a single morning and brought the United States into a global war.
reading: Japan and the United States had been on a collision course for years. Japan's leaders wanted an empire in East Asia and the oil, rubber and metals of Southeast Asia. The United States, which supplied most of Japan's oil, cut off those shipments in the summer of 1941 to force Japan out of China. Japan's military decided that if it was going to seize the oil of the Dutch East Indies it had to first cripple the American fleet based at *Pearl Harbor*, Hawaii. Talks in Washington continued while a fleet of six aircraft carriers steamed east in silence.

Just before eight on Sunday morning, December 7, 1941, the first wave of about one hundred eighty Japanese planes came over the mountains of Oahu. The American battleships were moored in a row. Within two hours, the attackers had sunk or badly damaged eight battleships and destroyed most of the aircraft on the island's airfields. About twenty-four hundred Americans were killed, nearly half of them on the battleship Arizona, which exploded and sank with more than a thousand men aboard. Japan lost twenty-nine planes. By luck, the American carriers were at sea and untouched.

The next day Roosevelt asked Congress to declare war, calling December 7 a date which will live in infamy. The vote was nearly unanimous. Three days later Germany and Italy, Japan's allies, declared war on the United States. The isolationist movement dissolved overnight; Lindbergh asked to fly combat missions. The country that had argued for two years about whether to fight was now at war on two oceans against three powers, with an army smaller than Portugal's had been a few years earlier.

Pearl Harbor also raised questions that historians still study. Why was the fleet caught by surprise when American code-breakers were reading Japanese diplomatic messages? The answer, most conclude, was not conspiracy but ordinary failure: warnings that were vague, sent too slowly or read by the wrong people. The attack taught a lesson that shaped American policy for the rest of the century. Never again, leaders decided, would the country be unprepared or wait for the enemy to strike first.

words.d: the U.S. naval base in Hawaii attacked by Japan on December 7, 1941
a government order stopping trade in certain goods with another country
a warship that launches and lands planes; the key weapon of the Pacific war

look.title: A Date Which Will Live in Infamy
look.text: Yesterday, December 7, 1941—a date which will live in infamy—the United States of America was suddenly and deliberately attacked by naval and air forces of the Empire of Japan.
look.cite: Franklin D. Roosevelt, address to Congress asking for a declaration of war, December 8, 1941
look.prompt: Roosevelt chose the words suddenly and deliberately. What is each word doing in the argument for war, and how does the sentence answer people who had wanted to stay out?

check.q: Why did Japan decide to attack the American fleet?
choices: To capture Hawaii as a colony
Because the United States had declared war on Japan
To end American aid to Britain
To cripple the fleet before seizing the oil of Southeast Asia after the U.S. cut off oil shipments
check.why: The American oil embargo pushed Japan's military to strike first at Pearl Harbor.

check.q: What piece of luck limited the damage at Pearl Harbor?
choices: The American aircraft carriers were at sea
The Japanese planes ran out of fuel
The battleships were in dry dock
The attack came on a weekday
check.why: The carriers survived to fight the Pacific war; the battleships were sunk or damaged.

check.q: What do most historians conclude about why the fleet was surprised?
choices: Roosevelt knew and let it happen
Japan had no plan until that morning
Ordinary failures: vague, slow or misread warnings
The code-breakers were spies
check.why: The evidence points to bureaucratic failure, not conspiracy.

lessons.title: Arsenal of Democracy
lessons.mainIdea: The war ended the Depression by turning the whole economy toward production, and the federal government directed it.
reading: The United States won the war partly with a weapon no other country could match: its factories. In 1939 American plants built a few thousand military aircraft. By 1944 they built almost a hundred thousand in a single year. Ford built a plant at Willow Run, Michigan, that turned out a four-engine bomber roughly every hour. Shipyards on the West Coast launched cargo ships in weeks instead of months. By the end of the war the United States had produced more weapons than all the Axis countries combined. Roosevelt called it the arsenal of democracy.

This did not happen by itself. The War Production Board, a federal agency, told companies what to make and what they could not make. No new cars were built for civilians from early 1942 until the war ended; the auto plants built tanks and planes. The government set prices, froze many wages and rationed scarce goods. Every family got *ration* books with stamps for sugar, coffee, meat, gasoline and shoes. Drivers had a sticker on the windshield showing how much gas they could buy. Americans grew vegetables in victory gardens and collected scrap metal and cooking fat for the war.

The war was paid for two ways. Taxes rose sharply, and for the first time most working Americans paid federal income tax, taken out of their paychecks. The rest was borrowed by selling *war bonds* to the public, with movie stars and schoolchildren leading the drives. Federal spending rose to about ninety billion dollars a year, ten times the level of the late 1930s. The Depression simply ended. Unemployment fell below two percent. Wages rose, and with little to buy, families saved.

The war also moved people. Millions left farms and small towns for jobs in Detroit, Los Angeles, Seattle and Chicago, which became a center of aircraft engine and munitions production. Hundreds of thousands of Black southerners came north in a second Great Migration. Mexican workers came under a program called the *bracero* agreement to fill farm jobs. Crowded cities, housing shortages and racial tension followed; in Detroit in 1943 a riot killed thirty-four people. The home front was not always united.

words.d: a fixed share of a scarce good that each person is allowed to buy
a loan from a citizen to the government, repaid with interest after the war
a Mexican worker brought to the United States under a wartime agreement to fill farm and railroad jobs
organizing a country's people and economy for war

look.title: Planes Built in the United States
look.cite: U.S. Army Air Forces statistical summaries, rounded
look.prompt: Production rose about fifty times in five years. What had to change in factories, in who worked, and in what the government could order for that to happen?

check.q: What did the War Production Board do?
choices: Ran the draft
Directed companies on what to make and stopped civilian car production
Set the price of war bonds
Built the Willow Run plant
check.why: The board turned the whole economy toward war goods by order, not by market choice.

check.q: How did most families experience rationing?
choices: They received free food from the government
They were forbidden to own cars
They used stamp books that limited how much sugar, meat and gasoline they could buy
They paid a tax on every purchase
check.why: Ration books and windshield stickers limited purchases of scarce goods.

check.q: What was one effect of war production on the Depression?
choices: Unemployment fell below two percent and the Depression ended
Unemployment rose because factories closed
Wages were cut in half
Farmers lost their land
check.why: Federal spending of about ninety billion dollars a year hired everyone who could work.

lessons.title: Women and War Work
lessons.mainIdea: With millions of men in uniform, women took factory jobs once closed to them, and the war changed ideas about women's work even though most were pushed out when it ended.
reading: About sixteen million Americans served in the armed forces during the war. Someone had to build the planes. Between 1940 and 1945 the number of women in paid work rose by roughly six million, to about nineteen million, and for the first time married women and mothers went to work in large numbers. They welded ship hulls, riveted bomber wings and ran drill presses. The government and the press celebrated the figure of Rosie the Riveter, a strong woman in coveralls with her sleeves rolled up. Posters told women that they could do it.

The reality was more complicated than the poster. Women were usually paid less than the men they replaced. Many employers hired them reluctantly and expected them to leave the moment the war ended. Child care was scarce; the government funded some centers, but most working mothers relied on relatives. Black women, who had mostly been limited to domestic work, fought for and won factory jobs, often in the least pleasant departments. Still, the paycheck and the skill were real. Many women said later that the war was the first time anyone had treated them as capable of serious work.

Women also served in uniform. About three hundred fifty thousand joined the women's branches of the Army, Navy, Coast Guard and Marines, mostly as clerks, mechanics, nurses and radio operators. About a thousand women flew military planes as ferry pilots and trainers in the *WASP* program, delivering aircraft from factories to bases so male pilots could go to combat. Thirty-eight of them died. They were considered civilians and were not granted veteran status until 1977.

When the war ended, the factories laid women off first to make room for returning soldiers, and government messages switched to urging women home. Most of the gains in factory work vanished within two years. Yet the share of women working never fell back to prewar levels, and the daughters of the Rosies grew up knowing what their mothers had done. Historians see the war less as a revolution than as a crack in the wall, one that the women's movement of the 1960s would widen.

words.d: the poster image of a woman factory worker used to recruit women during the war
the Women Airforce Service Pilots, civilian women who flew military planes within the United States
a metal pin hammered through sheets of metal to hold them together, as on an airplane

look.title: The Layoff Notice
look.text: In September 1945 a woman who has spent three years welding at a shipyard in Seattle, earning more than she ever thought possible, receives a notice that her job will go to a returning veteran. The newspaper that once called her a hero now runs articles about the importance of a well-kept home.
look.prompt: What arguments could she make for keeping her job, what could the veteran make, and what does the sudden change in the newspapers tell you about how the war's messages were designed?

check.q: About how many women were in paid work by 1945?
choices: About one million
About six million
About nineteen million
About sixty million
check.why: The number rose by roughly six million during the war to about nineteen million.

check.q: What did the WASP pilots do?
choices: Flew bombing missions over Germany
Ferried planes from factories to bases so male pilots could go to combat
Served as nurses on hospital ships
Trained as Navy officers
check.why: About a thousand women flew military aircraft within the United States; they were treated as civilians.

check.q: Why do historians call the war a crack in the wall rather than a revolution for women?
choices: Because no women worked in factories
Because women were paid more than men
Because women kept all their wartime jobs
Because most gains vanished after 1945, but the share of women working never fell back to prewar levels
check.why: The immediate change was rolled back, but the long-term shift and the memory endured.

lessons.title: Japanese American Incarceration
lessons.mainIdea: In 1942 the government removed about one hundred twenty thousand people of Japanese ancestry, most of them citizens, from the West Coast and held them in camps without charges.
reading: After Pearl Harbor, fear and old racism toward Asians on the West Coast combined into demands for action. Newspapers, politicians and some generals claimed that Japanese Americans might help an invasion, though no evidence of sabotage was ever found. On February 19, 1942, Roosevelt signed *Executive Order 9066*, which let the Army declare military zones and remove anyone from them. The Army used it against one group only. About one hundred twenty thousand people of Japanese ancestry living in California, Oregon, Washington and Arizona were ordered out. About two-thirds were American citizens by birth.

Families were given days, sometimes a week, to settle their affairs. They could take only what they could carry. Farms, shops and homes were sold for a fraction of their value or simply lost. People were first held at racetracks and fairgrounds, sleeping in horse stalls, then moved to ten camps in remote deserts and swamps from California to Arkansas. The camps had barbed wire, guard towers and barracks with no privacy. Schools, newspapers and baseball leagues sprang up inside, run by the prisoners themselves. Most stayed for about three years.

The government called it evacuation and relocation. The people inside, and most historians now, call it *incarceration*: imprisonment without charge or trial. In 1944 the Supreme Court upheld the removal in Korematsu v. United States, ruling that military necessity in wartime justified it. Three justices dissented. One wrote that the order fell into the ugly abyss of racism. Another warned that the ruling was a loaded weapon that any future government could pick up. Decades later the government admitted that the Army's claim of necessity had rested on false statements.

Meanwhile thousands of young men from the camps volunteered for the Army. The 442nd Regimental Combat Team, made up of Japanese Americans, fought in Italy and France and became one of the most decorated units of its size in American history. In 1988 Congress formally apologized and paid twenty thousand dollars to each surviving prisoner. The episode is studied as a test of what the Constitution means when a frightened country decides that one group is the enemy.

words.d: Roosevelt's 1942 order allowing the Army to remove people from military zones, used against Japanese Americans
imprisonment; the term most historians use for the wartime camps
a written opinion by a judge who disagrees with the court's majority
the 1944 Supreme Court case that upheld the removal of Japanese Americans

look.title: A Loaded Weapon
look.text: Justice Jackson, dissenting, warned that once a court approves a military order that discriminates by ancestry, the principle lies around like a loaded weapon, ready for the hand of any authority that can bring forward a plausible claim of urgent need.
look.cite: Robert H. Jackson, dissent in Korematsu v. United States, 1944 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Jackson was worried less about 1944 than about the future. What did he mean by a loaded weapon, and can you think of a later situation where his warning would apply?

check.q: What share of those removed were American citizens?
choices: Almost none
About one-tenth
About one-third
About two-thirds
check.why: Most of the roughly one hundred twenty thousand were citizens born in the United States.

check.q: How did the Supreme Court rule in Korematsu?
choices: It upheld the removal as a military necessity, with three justices dissenting
It ordered the camps closed immediately
It refused to hear the case
It ruled unanimously that the order was unconstitutional
check.why: The majority accepted the Army's claim of necessity; later evidence showed that claim was false.

check.q: Why do historians prefer the word incarceration to relocation?
choices: Because the camps were in cities
Because people were imprisoned without charge or trial behind barbed wire
Because the prisoners chose the term
Because relocation was a Japanese word
check.why: The government's word hid the fact that citizens were held under guard without any charges.

lessons.title: Europe: From North Africa to D-Day
lessons.mainIdea: The Allies defeated Germany by wearing it down on the Eastern Front, bombing it from the air and landing in France on June 6, 1944.
reading: The Allies agreed that Germany, not Japan, was the greater danger and had to be beaten first. But the biggest share of the fighting in Europe was done by the Soviet Union, which Germany had invaded in June 1941. On the Eastern Front, millions of soldiers fought along a line a thousand miles long. At Stalingrad, in the winter of 1942 to 1943, the Soviets surrounded and destroyed an entire German army. Roughly eight of every ten German soldiers who died in the war died fighting the Soviets. Stalin demanded that the Americans and British open a second front in France, and for two years they were not ready.

Instead the western Allies started at the edges. American troops landed in North Africa in November 1942 and, after early defeats, learned how to fight. They took Sicily in 1943 and pushed slowly up Italy against fierce resistance. Meanwhile American and British bombers attacked German cities and factories day and night. The bombing killed hundreds of thousands of civilians, and historians still debate how much it shortened the war. It did force Germany to pull fighters and guns back from the front to defend its cities.

The second front finally opened on June 6, 1944: *D-Day*. Under General Dwight Eisenhower, about one hundred fifty-six thousand American, British and Canadian troops crossed the English Channel and landed on five beaches in Normandy, France, in the largest seaborne invasion in history. At Omaha Beach, Americans came ashore under machine-gun fire from cliffs and took thousands of casualties in a single morning. By nightfall all five beaches were held. Within weeks a million Allied soldiers were in France. Paris was freed in August.

Germany struck back once, in December 1944, through the forests of Belgium in the Battle of the Bulge, the largest battle the U.S. Army fought in the war. American troops held, at a cost of about nineteen thousand killed. In the spring of 1945 the Allies crossed the Rhine from the west while the Soviets fought into Berlin from the east. Hitler killed himself on April 30. Germany surrendered on May 8, 1945, celebrated as V-E Day, victory in Europe.

words.d: the battle line between Germany and the Soviet Union, where most of the war's fighting in Europe took place
June 6, 1944, when Allied forces landed on the beaches of Normandy, France
a new battle line in western Europe that the Soviets demanded to take pressure off their armies
May 8, 1945, the day Germany's surrender took effect in Europe

look.title: The Dead, by Country
look.cite: Standard historians' estimates; Soviet and Chinese totals are especially uncertain
look.prompt: The United States fought on two oceans and lost about four hundred thousand people. What do these numbers say about who carried the war's heaviest weight, and how should that shape how Americans tell the story?

check.q: Where did most German soldiers who died in the war die?
choices: In North Africa
On the beaches of Normandy
Fighting the Soviet Union on the Eastern Front
In the Battle of the Bulge
check.why: Roughly eight in ten German military deaths came on the Eastern Front.

check.q: Why did the Allies attack North Africa and Italy before France?
choices: Because Italy had attacked Pearl Harbor
Because they were not yet ready for a full invasion of France
Because Stalin asked them to
Because Germany had no troops there
check.why: The western Allies built up strength and experience at the edges of Europe for two years before D-Day.

check.q: What was the Battle of the Bulge?
choices: Germany's last major attack in the west, in December 1944, which American troops held
The Soviet victory at Stalingrad
The Allied landing in Sicily
The bombing of Berlin
check.why: It was the largest battle the U.S. Army fought, costing about nineteen thousand American lives.

lessons.title: The Pacific: Island by Island
lessons.mainIdea: After turning the tide at Midway, the United States fought across the Pacific island by island in a brutal campaign that made an invasion of Japan look unbearable.
reading: For six months after Pearl Harbor, Japan won everywhere. It took the Philippines, where about seventy-five thousand American and Filipino prisoners were marched sixty-five miles with little food or water in the Bataan Death March, and thousands died. It took Singapore, the Dutch East Indies and islands across the Pacific. Then in June 1942 the Japanese navy tried to seize the tiny American base at *Midway*. American code-breakers had read the plan. In a single day American carrier planes sank four Japanese aircraft carriers. Japan never recovered the initiative.

The Pacific war was fought over water on a scale hard to imagine, and it was fought for islands, some no more than a mile long, that could hold an airfield. The American strategy was *island hopping*: seize the islands that mattered, bypass the rest and let their garrisons starve. Guadalcanal, Tarawa, Saipan, Iwo Jima, Okinawa. Each landing meant Marines wading ashore into gunfire from bunkers dug into coral and volcanic rock. Japanese soldiers were ordered never to surrender, and almost none did. On Iwo Jima in early 1945, about seven thousand Americans died to take eight square miles.

The fighting was marked by hatred on both sides that historians have called a war without mercy. Japanese forces committed atrocities against prisoners and civilians across Asia. American propaganda showed the Japanese as animals, and some American troops killed prisoners and took body parts as trophies. Meanwhile Navajo Marines used their own language as an unbreakable code, and Black units and Mexican American soldiers fought in a military that was still segregated.

Okinawa, from April to June 1945, was the worst. About twelve thousand Americans died, along with roughly a hundred thousand Japanese soldiers and a similar number of Okinawan civilians, many of whom were forced or persuaded to kill themselves rather than surrender. Japanese *kamikaze* pilots deliberately crashed planes into American ships. Planners looking at an invasion of Japan itself, scheduled for November 1945, expected casualties far beyond anything yet seen. That expectation shaped the decision you will read about in the next section.

words.d: the June 1942 battle in which American carrier planes sank four Japanese carriers and turned the Pacific war
the strategy of seizing key Pacific islands and bypassing others
a Japanese pilot who deliberately crashed a plane into an enemy ship
the troops stationed to defend a place

look.title: Two Miles of Sand
look.text: A planner in Washington in July 1945 lays out two maps. One shows Okinawa: eighty-two days of fighting, about twelve thousand Americans dead for one island. The other shows the Japanese home islands, with a population of over seventy million and an army being told to fight to the last person.
look.prompt: What would the planner conclude about an invasion, and what other options besides invasion or a new weapon might have been on the table? What would you want to know about each?

check.q: Why was Midway a turning point?
choices: Japan captured Hawaii
The United States sank four Japanese carriers and Japan lost the initiative
It was the first battle with kamikaze attacks
It ended the war in the Pacific
check.why: Code-breaking let the Americans ambush the Japanese fleet and destroy its carrier strength.

check.q: What was the goal of island hopping?
choices: To capture every island in the Pacific
To avoid all fighting
To seize islands that could hold airfields and bypass the rest
To defend Australia only
check.why: Key islands became bases for the next step, while bypassed garrisons were cut off.

check.q: How did Okinawa affect plans for invading Japan?
choices: It showed Japan was ready to surrender
It proved invasions were cheap
It had no effect on the plans
Its enormous cost made planners expect unbearable casualties in an invasion of Japan
check.why: About twelve thousand Americans and far more Japanese died for one island, and Japan was told to fight to the last.

lessons.title: The Holocaust and America's Response
lessons.mainIdea: Nazi Germany murdered six million Jews and millions of others, and the United States, which knew much of what was happening, did little to rescue them until late in the war.
reading: From the moment Hitler took power in 1933 the Nazi government stripped German Jews of their rights, their jobs and their property. After the war began, Germany's conquests placed millions more Jews under its control. Beginning in 1941, special units shot Jews by the hundreds of thousands in Eastern Europe, and in 1942 Germany built camps designed for killing. At Auschwitz and five other death camps in occupied Poland, trains arrived daily and most passengers were murdered in gas chambers within hours. By 1945 about six million Jews had been killed, along with millions of others: Poles, Soviet prisoners, Roma, disabled people, and gay men. We call this the *Holocaust*.

How much did Americans know? A great deal, and earlier than many later claimed. Reports of mass shootings reached newspapers in 1941 and 1942. In late 1942 the State Department confirmed a report that Germany planned to kill all the Jews of Europe, and the Allies publicly condemned it. But the news was often buried on inside pages, and many readers found it hard to believe. Before the war, the strict immigration quotas of 1924 kept most Jewish refugees out. In 1939 the ship St. Louis, carrying more than nine hundred Jewish refugees, was turned away from the United States and returned to Europe, where about a quarter of its passengers were later murdered.

The official position was that the fastest way to save the Jews was to win the war. Requests to bomb the rail lines to Auschwitz were refused as a diversion of resources, even though American bombers hit factories a few miles away in 1944. Officials in the State Department delayed rescue proposals and, in some cases, hid information. Only in January 1944, after Treasury officials documented that delay in a report to the president, did Roosevelt create the War Refugee Board. It helped save perhaps two hundred thousand people, largely in Hungary, proof of what earlier action might have done.

In April 1945 American troops reached camps like Ohrdruf, Buchenwald and Dachau and found the dead and the dying. General Eisenhower ordered soldiers, reporters and members of Congress to see it so that no one could later claim it had not happened. The Holocaust is studied as the extreme case of what a modern state can do, and America's response as a lesson about what a democracy owes to strangers in danger. The questions it raises are still argued whenever refugees ask for shelter.

words.d: the murder of about six million Jews and millions of others by Nazi Germany and its allies
the deliberate destruction of a whole people; a word coined in 1944 to describe crimes like the Holocaust
a person who flees their country to escape danger or persecution
the U.S. agency created in 1944 to rescue victims of Nazi persecution

look.title: Eisenhower Orders Witnesses
look.text: After visiting a camp in April 1945, Eisenhower wrote that the evidence of starvation, cruelty and bestiality was overwhelming. He said he had made the visit deliberately, so that he could give firsthand evidence if there ever grew up a tendency to charge that the stories were only propaganda.
look.cite: Dwight D. Eisenhower, cable to General George C. Marshall, April 1945 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Eisenhower was thinking about future deniers before the war was even over. Why did he think witnesses, photographs and reporters mattered so much, and what does that say about how history is defended?

check.q: When did the U.S. government confirm that Germany planned to murder all the Jews of Europe?
choices: Not until camps were found in 1945
In late 1942
In 1933, when Hitler took power
Never; it remained a rumor
check.why: The State Department confirmed the report in late 1942, and the Allies condemned the plan publicly.

check.q: What happened to the ship St. Louis in 1939?
choices: It was sunk by a German submarine
It landed its refugees in New York
It was turned away from the United States and returned to Europe
It carried soldiers to England
check.why: More than nine hundred Jewish refugees were refused entry, and about a quarter were later killed.

check.q: Why does the lesson call the War Refugee Board proof of what earlier action might have done?
choices: Because it saved perhaps two hundred thousand people in little more than a year
Because it bombed Auschwitz

lessons.title: The Manhattan Project
lessons.mainIdea: Fearing a German bomb, the United States built a secret atomic weapon in three years, and Chicago was where the key experiment happened.
reading: In 1939 scientists who had fled Nazi Germany learned that German physicists had split the uranium atom. Albert Einstein signed a letter to Roosevelt warning that Germany might build a bomb of unimaginable power. Roosevelt started a small research program. After Pearl Harbor it became the *Manhattan Project*, run by the Army under General Leslie Groves with the physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer leading the weapons laboratory. It would cost about two billion dollars, employ well over a hundred thousand people, and remain secret from nearly all of them. Most workers never knew what they were building.

Chicago's role came first. Fermi's pile under Stagg Field proved on December 2, 1942, that a controlled chain reaction was possible. That was the foundation for everything else. Huge plants were built in secret at Oak Ridge, Tennessee, to separate the rare kind of uranium that could be used in a bomb, and at Hanford, Washington, where giant reactors modeled on Fermi's pile produced a new element, *plutonium*. At Los Alamos, New Mexico, scientists designed the bombs themselves. Vice President Harry Truman, who had chaired a Senate committee on war spending, was told nothing until he became president in April 1945.

On July 16, 1945, in the desert of New Mexico, the first atomic bomb was tested. The explosion was brighter than the sun, and the blast was felt more than a hundred miles away. Oppenheimer later said a line from Hindu scripture had come to him: he had become death, the destroyer of worlds. Germany, the original reason for the project, had surrendered two months earlier and had never come close to a bomb. The weapon would now be used, if at all, against Japan.

Some of the Chicago scientists objected. In June 1945 a group led by James Franck sent a report arguing that using the bomb on a city without warning would start an arms race with the Soviet Union and cost the United States the world's trust. They proposed a demonstration on an empty island instead. Their report was set aside. A generation later some of the same scientists founded a magazine in Chicago whose cover carries a clock showing how close the world stands to catastrophe, a warning that has never been retired.

words.d: the secret American program from 1942 to 1945 that built the first atomic bombs
a process in which splitting atoms release neutrons that split more atoms, releasing energy
an element made in reactors and used in the bomb tested in New Mexico and dropped on Nagasaki
the splitting of an atom's nucleus, which releases energy

look.title: The Franck Report
look.text: Seven scientists in Chicago, June 1945. They know the bomb works on paper. They know Japan has no such weapon. They argue that if the United States drops it on a city with no warning, every other country will race to build one, and the United States will have shown the world that this is an acceptable way to fight.

To impress the Soviet Union

check.q: What did the Chicago experiment of December 1942 prove?
choices: That a controlled chain reaction was possible
That plutonium could be made at Hanford
That the bomb could be dropped from a plane
That uranium could be found in Illinois
check.why: Fermi's pile under Stagg Field was the foundation for the reactors and bombs that followed.

lessons.title: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
lessons.mainIdea: Two atomic bombs in August 1945 killed well over a hundred thousand people and ended the war, and the decision to use them is still debated on the evidence.
reading: On August 6, 1945, a single American plane dropped a uranium bomb on the city of Hiroshima. The blast, the heat and the fires destroyed most of the city in seconds. About seventy thousand people died that day, and tens of thousands more died from injuries and radiation sickness by the end of the year; the total is usually given as more than a hundred thousand. On August 9 a plutonium bomb fell on Nagasaki and killed at least forty thousand more. On the same day the Soviet Union, keeping a promise to the Allies, declared war on Japan and attacked its army in Manchuria.

On August 15 Japan's emperor announced surrender by radio, the first time most Japanese had heard his voice. The formal surrender was signed on an American battleship in Tokyo Bay on September 2, 1945. The war was over. In the United States the news brought crowds into the streets. Most Americans, and most soldiers waiting to invade Japan, believed the bomb had saved their lives, and polls at the time showed overwhelming approval.

Historians have argued ever since, and the argument turns on evidence. The case for the decision: Japan's leaders had rejected surrender demands, Okinawa showed what an invasion would cost, and even after Hiroshima the Japanese cabinet was deadlocked until the emperor intervened. The case against: Japan was already blockaded and starving, some Japanese leaders had been seeking peace through the Soviets, the United States refused to say whether the emperor could stay, and the Soviet attack may have mattered as much as the bombs. Some historians add that Truman also wanted to impress the Soviet Union. There is evidence for each claim, and no document settles it.

What is not in doubt is what the bombs did. The survivors, called *hibakusha* in Japanese, suffered burns, cancers and stigma for the rest of their lives, and many of them spent those lives telling the world what they had seen. The United States has never used a nuclear weapon since, and neither has anyone else, but nine countries now have them. The question the Chicago scientists asked in June 1945 became the central question of the next fifty years.

words.d: the Japanese city destroyed by the first atomic bomb on August 6, 1945
Japanese word for the survivors of the atomic bombings
giving up with no terms or promises from the winning side
illness caused by exposure to the invisible energy released by a nuclear explosion

look.title: Truman Announces the Bomb
look.text: In a statement released from the White House, Truman announced that an American plane had dropped one bomb on Hiroshima with more power than twenty thousand tons of TNT. He said it was an atomic bomb, a harnessing of the basic power of the universe, and warned that if Japan did not surrender, it could expect a rain of ruin from the air.
look.cite: Harry S. Truman, statement announcing the use of the atomic bomb, August 6, 1945 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Truman's statement calls Hiroshima a military base and promises more attacks. Who were the audiences for this statement, and what was each one meant to conclude?

check.q: What else happened on August 9, 1945, besides the Nagasaki bomb?
choices: Germany surrendered
The Soviet Union declared war on Japan and attacked in Manchuria
Japan's emperor spoke on the radio
The Manhattan Project was announced
check.why: The Soviet attack is one reason historians debate how much the bombs alone caused the surrender.

check.q: Which is part of the case for using the bomb?
choices: Japan was already blockaded and starving
Truman wanted to impress the Soviets
Even after Hiroshima the Japanese cabinet was deadlocked until the emperor intervened
The United States refused to promise the emperor could stay

choices: Because all the records were destroyed
Because historians refuse to study it
Because Truman never wrote anything down

check.why: Historians weigh competing evidence about whether Japan would have surrendered without the bombs.

lessons.title: A New World and the GI Bill
lessons.mainIdea: The war left the United States the richest and most powerful nation on earth, committed to a new United Nations and to sending millions of veterans to college.
reading: When the shooting stopped, the world had changed shape. Britain and France were exhausted. Germany and Japan lay in ruins under occupation. China was sliding into civil war. Only two countries came out stronger: the Soviet Union, with the largest army in the world and control of Eastern Europe, and the United States, whose factories were untouched and whose economy produced about half of everything made on earth. The United States alone had the atomic bomb. These two powers, allies for four years, would soon be enemies for forty.

Roosevelt had died in April 1945, but his plan for the peace went forward. In June 1945 fifty countries met in San Francisco to sign the charter of the *United Nations*, an organization meant to succeed where the League of Nations had failed after World War I. Its Security Council gave the five main victors, including the United States and the Soviet Union, a veto over its actions. Unlike 1919, the Senate approved American membership overwhelmingly. Trials at Nuremberg put surviving Nazi leaders before an international court for war crimes and crimes against humanity, setting a precedent that still shapes international law.

At home, Congress had planned ahead. The Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, known as the *GI Bill*, offered every returning veteran money for college or job training, low-interest loans to buy a home or start a business, and a year of unemployment pay. About eight million veterans used the education benefit. Colleges that had served the wealthy filled with the sons of factory workers and farmers. Home loans built the suburbs. Economists count the GI Bill among the best investments the government ever made.

The bill's promise was not equal. It was administered locally, and in the South, and often in the North, Black veterans were steered away from colleges, denied loans by banks and shut out of new suburbs by rules that barred Black buyers. About a million Black Americans had served. Their exclusion from much of the GI Bill's wealth is one root of the gap in family wealth that persists today. The war made the United States a superpower and built its middle class, and it left the question of who belonged to that middle class for the next generation to fight over.

words.d: the international organization founded in 1945 to keep peace and settle disputes among nations
the 1944 law giving veterans money for college, home loans and unemployment pay
a nation with enough military and economic strength to shape events worldwide
the trials of Nazi leaders after the war for war crimes and crimes against humanity
